The proposed answer of 51 is incorrect, because it misses several valid values of n.

**Setup.** Call the relation "friends" F and "enemies" R. The condition says: if A is an enemy of B and B is a friend of C, then A is an enemy of C.

**Friendship is an equivalence relation.**
- Suppose B and C are friends and A is an enemy of B. Then A is an enemy of C. By symmetry, friends B and C have exactly the same set of enemies.
- Suppose B–C and C–D are friends. B, C and D then all have the same enemy set. If B and D were enemies, D would be in B's enemy set, which equals C's enemy set. That would make C and D enemies, a contradiction. So B and D are friends, and friendship is transitive.

**Structure.** The guests split into friend-cliques, and every pair from different cliques are enemies. Each guest's enemies are everyone outside their own clique, so each clique has size s with n − s = 12. Hence n = 12 + s.

**Divisibility.** The cliques all have size s and partition the n guests, so s divides n = 12 + s. This means s divides 12, so s ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12}.

This gives n ∈ {13, 14, 15, 16, 18, 24}. Each of these works, since a complete multipartite enemy graph with equal parts of size s satisfies the condition.

**Sum.** 13 + 14 + 15 + 16 + 18 + 24 = 100.

The proposed solution lists only 13, 14 and 24. It omits 15, 16 and 18, which come from cliques of size 3, 4 and 6.

VERDICT: REJECT
